passages.t: ‘Be not deaf to me, O my Rock’, and ‘He has heard’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “Of David” (verse 1). He calls out, afraid of God's silence: “To You, O LORD, I call; be not deaf to me, O my Rock. For if You remain silent, I will be like those descending to the Pit” (verse 1).

“Hear my cry for mercy when I call to You for help, when I lift up my hands toward Your holy sanctuary” (verse 2). He asks not to be dragged away with false people “who speak peace to their neighbors while malice is in their hearts” (verse 3), and asks God to repay them for what they have done (verse 4).

Then the psalm turns. “Blessed be the LORD, for He has heard my cry for mercy” (verse 6). “The LORD is my strength and my shield; my heart trusts in Him, and I am helped” (verse 7).

It ends with a prayer for the whole people: “Save Your people and bless Your inheritance; shepherd them and carry them forever” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
This is a lament that turns to thanks. He calls God ‘my Rock’, the solid place that does not move, and yet the rock seems silent. ‘The Pit’ was a word for a cistern or a dungeon, and in poetry for the grave. For this man, God's silence feels like the first step towards death.

Raising open hands was the usual way to pray. Verse 2 adds where he faces: toward God's ‘holy sanctuary’, the innermost room of the temple. Israelites far from it turned toward it to pray, as Solomon asked God to hear those who “pray toward this place” (1 Kings 8:30).

Some readers think a priest spoke a word of comfort between verses 5 and 6, as some think of Psalm 6. Others think the change happened as he prayed. The psalm does not say.
passages.later:
Paul wants believers “to pray, lifting up holy hands, without anger or dissension” (1 Timothy 2:8).

Verse 3's two-faced neighbours appear in Jesus' warning about false prophets: “They come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves” (Matthew 7:15). And verse 9's shepherd who carries his people is the God of Isaiah 40:11, who “gathers the lambs in His arms”.
passages.hard: Verse 4 asks God to repay the wicked. This belongs with the hard prayers the book page treats in ‘The cursing psalms’. Notice that the man asks God to judge. He does not take revenge himself.
passages.asks:
Is God's silence frightening you? The psalm lets you say so, and keep calling.

Notice that he does not wait for an answer before he says ‘He has heard’. Trust can speak before the proof arrives.

The psalm also ends where many personal prayers forget to go: with the whole people. When God has heard you, pray verse 9 for others.
